#6694. Jensen Huang Traded His Leather Jacket for a Humble Cotton Zip-Up During His Nvidia Return

Jensen Huang is back in. The leather jackets? They’re out. The disgraced former Nvidia CEO reclaimed the top job at the American tech giant yesterday, returning to a big welcome from employees and even the president himself. (Trump told CNBC that he “made the deal” to get Huang back in as CEO.) But as Huang returned to the office where he became a billionaire, something was noticeably different. His gray hair remained neatly side-parted as ever, but his usual standout outerwear was swapped for something a whole lot humbler: a navy cotton jacket.

Or, sort of humbler, anyway. Subtle as it may be, Huang’s zip-up appears to nonetheless hail from luxury designer Dior. (The label did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation or comment.) The $3,300 number is the brand’s zippered shirt, one that he’s actually worn in the past, notably when he landed at Gimpo International Airport in Seoul in June of this year. (That was the same trip during which he got memed for wearing a leather jacket on one of the city’s sweatiest summer days.)

The 63-year-old, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, wore high-end black leather jackets as his daily uniform for over a decade. In September, he told CBS News he owned between 30 to 40, from brands like Tom Ford, Burberry, Dior, and Dunhill. At a Stanford economic summit in 2024, Huang offered up a very practical, Silicon Valley-esque reason for his leather preference: They don’t make him itch. But they also felt like an intentional effort to use fashion to break beyond the tech industry’s traditionally geeky image, à la Mark Zuckerberg sitting front row at Prada or Adam Mosseri showing up at the Met Gala in Kartik Research.

Following the revelation of his extramarital affairs, however—most notably with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as with at least two Nvidia employees—the garments took on a new meaning. Rather than evoking the likes of James Dean or Marlon Brando, the lush outerwear instead began to suggest a man in the throes of a midlife crisis.

Huang’s return as CEO isn’t unprecedented. For example, OpenAI’s Sam Altman was reinstated after employees revolted against the board’s initial firing of the CEO. The move does, however, raise concerns about national security and Nvidia’s company culture.

The dismissal of the leather jacket marks a new chapter in Huang’s tenure at the helm of Nvidia. It had always been a talking point, and after becoming a symbol of his fall from grace, wearing it again would risk turning it into his own scarlet letter. By swapping out stiff leather for easy, approachable cotton, Huang seems to be signaling the desire for a reset. As he told his staff during his return: “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

#6693. The 10 Best Lipsticks for Women Over 40 That Deliver Instant Hydration and Lasting Color

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

A swipe of lipstick is one of the easiest ways to look instantly put together with minimal effort. Even if you have nothing else on your face, a hint of lip color can lift your complexion. It also works as an accessory or finishing touch for even the simplest outfits.

As we get older, lips naturally feel drier and lose volume. A good balm nourishes and comforts parched lips, but if you want more pigment, many lipsticks are designed for mature skin.

First, steer clear of ultra-matte formulas, as they tend to dehydrate lips and highlight every fine lip line imaginable. They also tend to look flat.

For extra long wear, try a velvety, soft-matte formula instead. It delivers a similar, statement-making finish that's elegant while creating a pillowy, plush effect.

Satin formulas perform well, too. The gentle shine creates the illusion of healthier-looking lips, and it feels less drying throughout the day. That said, brighter shades like reds and oranges can be a little messy to apply, so apply one layer, blend with a fingertip, and blot with a tissue. Repeat to build intensity. If feathering (when the color "bleeds" into fine lines around your lips) is an issue, a clear lip liner around the perimeter should create a barrier.

It's always best to get your skincare benefits from your lip balm, but nourishing plant oils and hydrating ingredients such as glycerin and hyaluronic acid in your lipstick will help maintain hydration as the day goes on.

For makeup artist and Jones Road founder Bobbi Brown, there are no hard-and-fast rules—no matter your age. "It's about your style, what you feel most comfortable in," she tells Bazaar UK.

If you're keen on neutral tones, remember that neutral doesn't mean beige. "Pay attention to what your natural lip color is. I have a slightly bluish-purple tone to my lips. You might have more of a pink tone. It's really great to find a lipstick that really looks like your lips, and the only way is to test it on your bottom lip," says Brown, who notes that a great neutral should not wash you out.

Revered makeup artist Bobbi Brown is no stranger to creating iconic lipsticks. The Classic Lip has all the hallmarks of a modern formula: creamy, intensely hydrating, and richly pigmented. The 12-color range offers enough variety without overwhelming consumers. Expect skin-enhancing neutrals and bolder tones for any occasion.

Trinny London excels at makeup for mature skin, and this recent launch is certainly no exception. It's a glossy, mega-hydrating formula that reflects light beautifully, making lips look plumper, and it's formulated with peptides to help reduce fine lines over time. There's a full spectrum of nude shades, but we love the bold red Poppy for festive nights.

A richly pigmented, buttery-smooth formula that promises to minimize dryness without sacrificing impact. It contains plenty of nourishing oils to keep moisture lasting without feathering into fine lines. It has a rosy scent, so keep that in mind if you're sensitive to fragrance.

Everything Victoria Beckham does delivers instant polish to the lips without extra effort. This slimline lipstick is no exception. It glides on like a tinted lip balm, adding a touch more color while infusing skin with hydration. VB has perfected the art of neutrals, so expect to find easy-to-wear hues for all skin tones. Glide on, then pat to blend any hard edges. It's one of those formulas you won't need a mirror to apply.

Refillable makeup isn't new, but Lisa Eldridge has painstakingly ensured every part of her Rouge Experience lipstick is recyclable, while it still looks like it belongs on a movie star's dresser. The lipstick formula combines oil, gel, and cream to ensure all-day comfort. The color pigments build easily and sit between a soft matte and a shiny finish. It's unfragranced, too.

Creative and image director of Christian Dior Makeup, Peter Philips, reviewed Dior's bestselling lip colors worldwide to create a tightly curated collection of 10 sophisticated, wearable shades for every skin tone. Nude doesn't mean beige, according to Philips, and this line includes a complexion-lifting neutral, whatever that looks like to you. The emollient formula glides on like balmy, satin lipstick but won't budge once it sets. Expect long-wear color without the drying side effects.

When Hourglass creates matte lipsticks, rest assured they feature elevated colors and sit beautifully on the lips without highlighting fine lines, feathering, or flaking. This elegant formula feels velvety soft, with buildable pigments that stay put.

Sisley's interpretation of a shimmery, luminous lip color is as elevated as you've come to expect from this storied French brand. Phyto Rouge Shine is infused with the finest pearlescent particles in a translucent base, delivering sheer, buildable color and a plumping effect that still looks understated and grown-up.

Hermès Beauty creative director Gregoris Pyrpylis drew inspiration from Hermès scarves when designing this collection. This translates into buildable, luminous color and a smooth, tactile finish that feels like a second skin. Even the deepest shades look refined, with a radiance that brightens the face. Plus, the wide, angled bullet makes application as easy as wearing a lip balm.

Not all liquid lipsticks are created equal. Violette's soft, whipped texture is truly modern, delivering intense colors without a heavy feel. The gel-cream texture blurs out fine lines, too, so lips appear plush and smooth.

#6692. How One Live-Wire Stylist Puts His Meta Glasses to Work on Set

When Meta announced the latest generation of its genre-defining smart glasses, the response from the fashion industry was, well, kind of tepid. Wearable technology has a shaky track record, after all, and we’ve been down a similar road before. (Google Glass, we hardly knew thee.) To win over folks more fluent in Ai Weiwei than AI, Meta would have to fulfill a much trickier mandate than simply developing a groundbreaking product: it’d have to develop a product that looks good while doing the ground breaking.

So when I got the chance to put Meta Glasses to the test during a typically frenetic day on set shooting for GQ, I didn’t hold back. It helps, obviously, that they actually look cool—especially the limited-edition pair I requested, a collaboration with the chart-topping Blackpink member LISA. Now, though, I’m convinced of their genuine, potentially game-changing utility, too. Here’s how I put the Meta Glasses by LISA through the paces of my chaotic 9-to-5, and emerged all the less stressed for it.

On shoot days, I make a point of arriving on set an hour before our model so I can lock in our looks with minimal distraction. The clothes on the racks, though, tend to play second fiddle to the clothes on me, at least when it comes to my AM fit check. (Like a true sicko, I wore a fluorescent Prada jacket to match the pink tint on my special-edition, LISA-designed Meta Glasses.)

Without fail, every shoot I’ve been on comes together very dynamically—read: absolutely last minute. So even though we boarded each look weeks ago, and styled them all out yesterday afternoon, no fewer than 15-ish items arrived that morning. To sort through them, I tell Meta to put on the new Sophia Stel album so I can lock in and land on the right roster of looks.

The looks have been landed on—it’s time to present them to the team. GQ commerce director Michael Nolledo—the magnanimous Miranda Priestly of the entire operation, if you will—is off-site for the day, so I tell Meta to video call him for approval. He can now see what I see, and I stay totally hands-free.

During the run through, I describe each look down to its socks, clarifying the logic behind my styling decisions with near-comical specificity. (Yes, that minuscule sliver of waffle thermal peeking out from beneath that fleece is, in fact, transformative and entirely nonnegotiable!) I tend to love this part of the day because the looks always end up in a sometimes-different-always-better place once the braintrust has weighed in—and tempered some of my, uh, kookier impulses.

It doesn’t matter how nice the clothes look hanging limply on the rack: they don’t really come to life (or die in front of your very eyes) until you get them on the guy. Luckily, our guy for the day is Gabriel, whose easy, unaffected chill makes everything we put him in look effortlessly incredible.

As we noodle on a few minor alternations (bringing in a suit jacket just-so; adding hefty cuffs to a pair of appropriately hefty trousers), I have Meta snap a photo of each look in its final form. On my command, Meta then sends those photos to Michael and GQ senior editor Avidan Grossman—my closest collaborator on set and our in-house tailoring geek—who has final say on all things pleated pants, dimpled ties, and more. Once Meta beams out the fitting photos, it’s speak now or forever hold your peace.

The next six hours are a frenetic blur, set to a fittingly chaotic blend of ‘80s pop hits and Tate McRae (it’s all about balance, really). Beth, our prodigiously talented photographer for the day, becomes my partner, as we both try to ensure Gabriel ignores the camera as much as possible. The best photos happen when the guy forgets he’s being photographed—like we’re capturing a genuine moment of relaxed solitude.

Problem is, when I’m laser-focused on all that, I hate pulling out my phone to capture content of my own. So the option to have Meta snap a fast photo or record a snippet of video is kind of a godsend.

We made it, folks. Three green teas, four minor hand injuries, and 18 or so looks later, it’s time for the fun part: reviewing the photos, and duking it out over which of them will make the final cut. There really is no greater satisfaction than seeing a slapdash deck of product flats transform into an all-killer, no-filler album of actual outfits.

Because I have no patience (and am beaming with so much pride it's nearly blinding), I have Meta snap a few shots of my favorite moments and then post them to my IG story. The official GQ story won’t run for a few weeks, so I like to think of my story as an unofficial teaser of sorts. We pack up and roll our racks out of the studio and back into the fashion closet, where I promptly ask Meta for directions to the closest bar.

While brunettes might need less frequent touch-ups than blondes, any chemically colored hair still needs care and attention. “The best way to treat freshly coloured hair at home is to always use a professional color protect shampoo and conditioner,” Green explained. “It’s also important to avoid using too much heat,” she added.

#6689. Two Menswear Darlings Just Made the Most Covetable Boots of 2026

Say you wanted to create the perfect pair of vintage-style military boots. First, you’d need a designer with impeccable taste and encyclopedic knowledge of vintage workwear; then you'd need a bootmaker with the requisite skills to produce it at the highest level. If everything went right, the result would be something like the Modèle 1917, a new collaboration between famed Parisian creative director Gauthier Borsarello and renowned Canadian bootmaker Viberg.

In basic terms, the Modèle 1917 is a pair of boots based on the French Army’s 1917 “brodequin,” a design used by soldiers in the trenches of WWI, available in soft brown suede (Mud) and glossy textured black leather (Pavement). But there’s nothing basic about them. The design comes courtesy of Borsarello, a top-tier collector of vintage workwear and the creative mind behind Gersaint Paris and L’Etiquette magazine. Viberg, a third-generation, family-owned boot specialist, got its start making footwear for forestry crews in British Columbia, and it still builds every pair in its Vancouver Island workshop. While it doesn’t make boots for smokejumpers and loggers anymore, old-school shoemaking techniques like a channeled insole Goodyear welt and stitchdown construction ensure their footwear retains its heirloom-level durability.

The backstory of the “brodequin” begins with the Mdl. 1893, a hobnail-soled marching boot created for French infantrymen in the late 1800s that remained in use until the 1950s. In the First World War, the brodequin’s iron-studded soles and sturdy uppers proved ideally suited to the muddy conditions of the trenches, and American troops soon adopted them in place of their inferior M1904 Marching Shoes. “To me, it’s the blueprint for many combat boots across different countries after WWI,” says Borsarello. “I love the idea that France inspired others after fighting side by side in the trenches. They’re very simple, yet instantly recognizable at the same time.”

For all of its strengths in the field, the original brodequin—whose nickname pays tongue-in-cheek homage to a medieval torture device—wasn’t what you’d call a comfortable boot, especially by modern standards. “They were so stiff that they were almost impossible to walk in,” Borsarello admits. This created something of a design challenge.

To stay as true as possible to the original, Borsarello and Viberg designed the boots on a period-correct “pied haricot” (bean-shaped) last, with a cotton twill lining, solid brass hardware, and reinforced panels that support the midfoot so the forefoot can move freely. To make the Modèle M1917 something you’d actually want to wear, they replaced the hobnailed soles with rubber ones and swapped the original roughout leather for supple American-tanned Horween. The result is a pair of boots that are as comfortable as they are durable, not to mention surprisingly versatile. In other words, exactly what you’d expect from a meeting of these formidable talents.

#6685. 24 Veil Alternatives for the Bride Who’d Rather Skip Tradition

Some brides consider the wedding veil sacred, whether it’s an heirloom passed down through generations or a sweeping cathedral-length piece they’ve dreamed of since childhood. Others would rather skip tradition altogether, opting for a statement hair accessory in lieu of lace and tulle. Fortunately, there’s no shortage of veil alternatives—and while they’re a natural fit for courthouse weddings, elopements, and intimate vow exchanges, they can easily hold their own at more formal celebrations, too. Take Princess Eugenie, who ditched the veil entirely for her 2018 nuptials, letting a borrowed emerald tiara steal the show. (If a royal can forgo tradition, so can you!) More recently, Dua Lipa paired a custom Schiaparelli suit with a wide-brimmed Stephen Jones hat for her London civil ceremony.

Bridal designers are also going veil-free: Recent collections from Honor, Floure Studio, Vivienne Westwood, House of Gilles, and Elie Saab feature everything from sculptural hats to bows. When picking out your accessory for the big day, think about balance. An ivory headband adds a modern touch to an otherwise classic ball gown. A lace cloche dials up the drama on a minimalist dress, while a flowing, floral-embroidered scarf brings a romantic feel to a courthouse mini. Wearing a suit? A pillbox hat keeps things incredibly chic, whether you’re getting married at City Hall or eloping somewhere far-flung. Once you’ve settled on a style, be sure to bring it to your hair trial so your stylist knows how to incorporate your accessory seamlessly.

Ahead, discover 24 wedding veil alternatives for every type of bride.

Few accessories are as foolproof as a bridal headband, and with so many iterations on the market, it’s easy to find one that feels right for you. Unadorned padded styles from Loeffler Randall and Maison Ola draw instant attention to a low bun or sleek blowout, while a hand-embroidered option from Lock & Co. Hatters adds some sparkle.

If you’re planning a courthouse wedding or just want an accessory with real presence, a bridal hat is hard to beat. These wide-brimmed silhouettes from Maison Michel, Mains de Vapeur, and Eugenia Kim bring all the drama (and welcome shade at an outdoor ceremony). For something smaller, Gigi Burris’s pillbox has a lovely vintage-inspired aesthetic.

Juliet caps, cloches, and jeweled headpieces are heirlooms in the making; unlike delicate tulle, they’re sturdy enough to be passed down and worn again—plus, they have a built-in old-world feel. Alexandra Grecco and Jennifer Behr keep things soft with lace; De La Vali goes all out with a headscarf that drapes elegantly mid-back; Rabanne channels ’20s glamour with a pearl-and-bead design.

Not ready to surrender the movement of a veil? A cape or scarf offers a similar effect—just in a less conventional way. Rat & Boa’s sheer style shimmers with hand-embellished sequins, and Clio Peppiatt’s mini version adds beaded fringe for extra swing. To keep things understated, drape Markarian’s embroidered scarf or Heirlome’s silk stole over your shoulders.

Bows and bridal have always gone hand in hand, and they make for a playful hair accessory for the consummate romantic. These options from Vivienne Westwood, Completedworks, and Oscar de la Renta fit cascading curls especially well. For a subtle nod to the classic veil, go with Kamperett’s oversized piece, which trails all the way to the floor.

Trade your bouquet for blooms in your hair—or (why not!) go all out and wear both. From flower crowns to smaller clips and pins, there are endless ways to work florals into your hairstyle, especially if you consider yourself a boho bride, and picked the pastoral venue to prove it.

#6680. These Were the Breakout Red Carpet Stars of 2026

Whew—what a year it’s been for red carpets, huh? Between awards season, Fashion Month, and Vogue’s weekly celebrity roundups, there’s been plenty of statement looks to take in throughout 2026. And while there were some notable A-list standouts this year—especially those on our annual Best Dressed list—there were also plenty of emerging names who proved their status as notable rising stars.

Below, Vogue rounded up the 10 breakout stars who had especially splashy, career-making years. And better yet, these buzzy actors and singers all come armed with a unique red carpet style. Whether it’s North of North star Anna Lambe’s championing of Indigenous designers, or actor Diego Calva’s slick array of suits worn on his Club Kid press tour, these Hollywood names are making their mark with distinct fashion choices that make them stand out from the pack. (Sure, they have a team of agents and stylists—but you simply can’t buy taste.)

So, without further ado, meet Vogue’s 10 breakout red carpet stars of 2026.

North of North star Anna Lambe was busy promoting the second season of her hit Netflix series this year—and the Indigenous (Inuk) star brought a unique flavor to the red carpets, working with stylist Nadia Pizzimenti. When she wasn’t busy championing Indigenous designers such as Jamie Okuma or Lesley Hampton, you could find her slipping into sleek Louis Vuitton leather pieces—and sitting front row at the show, of course (like a true fashion It girl).

The Scottish actor gained buzz when he joined the Marvel universe this year, starring in the Disney+ series VisionQuest—but his personal style on the red carpet has been just as action-packed as the show. He and his stylist Fabio Immediato have been showcasing how cool, modern, and totally unfussy modern tailoring can be. Those tinted Prada shades at a VisionQuest screening! A fun little Valentino tie at the BAFTA Scotland Awards! Let’s hear it for a man who has fun with dressing up.

What happens when you star in one of the biggest Hollywood franchises, well, ever? Actor Whitney Peak would know: She brought some seriously epic blockbuster fashions to The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour this year. The star and her stylist Karla Welch have leaned into designs that are theatrical and extravagant—a perfect mood for promoting the film, given the Capitol in The Hunger Games is all about excess. Come for the chic Chanel gowns—stay for the Robert Wun bird dress.

Mexican actor Diego Calva may have gained attention for his role as a social worker in Club Kid, but his red carpet style is less club-rat and much more sleek, sexy and refined. He and stylist Ilaria Urbinati’s go-to formula? Injecting classic-cut suits with more unexpected details. Like his bright red Dzojchen suit and polka-dot tie, or black Loewe tuxedo with a bright-yellow shirt and tie. It’s hard to give a timeless two-piece a more irreverent personality, but Calva has it in spades.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you’ve come across a dance banger by Adéla this year. (Finish the lyric: “Every single night, I pray that. . .”) The singer has had a breakout year, thanks to her hits-filled album Prima—so much so that she’s playing Coachella next year. And just as stage-worthy is her pop star approach to fashion. Working with stylist Chris Horan (a master of pop style), she’s cultivated a signature look surrounding tight corsets, mini shorts, and of course, her bright pink hair.

You may know Owen Thiele as a pro podcaster (stream “In Your Dreams”) and actor (watch Adults), but the rising star is bringing some sleek attitude to the red carpet scene. He’s been working with stylist Jared Ellner (his IRL boyfriend, fun fact), and his wardrobe for the spotlight centers around giving menswear classics a more youthful twist. Think: A suit vest worn with no shirt underneath, or a classic collared shirt with more than a few buttons unbuttoned. Fierce is fierce, honey.

It’s certainly Sienna Spiro’s year, thanks to her acclaimed debut album Visitor. The English singer won best new artist at this year’s MTV VMAs—and earned the same award nomination at the 2026 Grammys, no less. If one can describe her sound as raspy and powerful, her red carpet style can be labelled as just as soulful: She works with stylist Edie Rose to find looks that are sweet and slightly retro, pulling archival references (or full-on vintage) pieces that give her a distinctive edge.

With a commanding name like Guitarricadelafuente, the Spanish singer and actor almost has to have a bold sense of style to match. And he certainly does: The star, who is garnering early Oscar buzz for his role in this year’s La Bola Negra, has been making the press rounds in striking looks all masterminded by stylist Luca Guarini. His casual little Marni V-neck sweater at the GQ Men of the Year Awards! His sleek black Dior tuxedo at the Governor Awards! Get you a man that can do both.

When you’re playing a Disney princess like Moana, your red carpet style has to be just as enchanting—and Samoan-Australian actor Catherine Laga’aia understood this assignment fully. While promoting her live-action reboot of the beloved franchise, the actor and her stylist Alexandra Mandelkorn embraced the tropical, beachy feel of the film—with lightweight summery frocks that struck the right balance of red carpet appropriate yet utterly effortless. From the gauzy white laces to the summery polkadots, her cheery style is a breath of fresh air.

From Not Suitable for Work to season three of The White Lotus, we could simply not escape Nicholas Duvernay on our TV screens this year—not that we’re complaining about it. The star and his stylist Avo Yermagyan have subverted menswear codes to make the silhouettes and details just a touch more intriguing. A three-buttoned tan blazer from DSquared2? Check. A plaid Wooyoungmi suit with a pop-of-red shirt? Check. Serious suiting swagger? Check-check.

#6676. Who Is Malin Akerman’s Husband, Jack Donnelly?

The Hunting Wives star married the British actor in 2018

Malin Akerman may stir up romantic trouble as Margo Banks, the notorious ringleader of The Hunting Wives, but off screen, her love life is much less chaotic. The actress has been happily married to fellow actor Jack Donnelly since 2018, and over the years, the two have even found ways to merge their professional and personal lives.

Akerman and Donnelly have collaborated on several projects, including four movies (and an NSFW sex scene, but more on that below). In a 2023 interview with People, the actress opened up about their relationship, crediting her husband with helping her become a better communicator.

“He’s allowed me to be vulnerable and lean into him a bit, and it’s been beautiful to be able to communicate with someone who’s your partner,” she said of their marriage.

Ahead, everything you need to know about Jack Donnelly, his career, and his marriage with Akerman.

Donnelly was born in Bournemouth, England, on October 28, 1985, and later attended the Central School of Speech and Drama in London. He made his acting debut in 2011 on the Nickelodeon series House of Anubis. Two years later, he landed a breakout lead role in the BBC’s series Atlantis, as Jason—which remains one of his best-known roles to date.

In addition to acting, Donnelly has branched out behind the camera as a television writer and director. He wrote, directed, and starred in the short comedy series The Players, which debuted in 2023.

The couple’s love story began with a family connection. Donnelly first met Akerman through her younger sister, whose boyfriend was friends with him at drama school. During a 2018 appearance on Live With Kelly and Ryan, the actress explained that she had actually known Donnelly for several years before their relationship turned romantic.

“I had known him for the past four years but didn’t see him,” she recalled. “Then all of a sudden he came back from England like a year-and-a-half ago, and I went, ‘Wow, have you always been this cute?’”

Akerman announced the couple’s engagement via Instagram in October 2017. Sharing a selfie with Donnelly and flashing her new engagement ring, she captioned the post, “This sweet and loving man has stepped into our lives and stole both our hearts,” she wrote, referring to her and her son. “I think we’re gonna keep him around for a while,” she continued with a wink.

Akerman and Donnelly tied the knot a little over a year later, on December 1, 2018, in a beach ceremony held in Tulum, Mexico. “It was all about being authentic...not adhering to somebody else’s standard of what a wedding should be,” Akerman told Brides.

“We wanted something beautiful and lush,” she continued, sharing more about their wedding venue. “When we visited Papaya Playa Project [in Tulum], we fell in love with the boho vibes and beach setting.”

In 2023, Akerman shared new photos from the beachside wedding on Instagram to celebrate their five-year anniversary.

When discussing her engagement on Live With Kelly and Ryan in 2018, Akerman also shared how excited her son, Sebastian, was about the news. The actress shares Sebastian with her ex-husband, musician Roberto Zincone, and recalled his excited reaction when she told him that she and Donnelly were getting married. “He jumped up on the couch and went, ‘Yay, we’re getting married!’” she said.

In another 2018 interview with Us Weekly, Akerman gushed about the close bond Donnelly had already formed with her then-five-year-old son. “They’re inseparable,” she said. “It makes my heart warm. I’m very glad to be bringing Jack into our lives for good.”

Over the years, the three have also made several red-carpet appearances together, offering a glimpse into their life as a family.

Akerman and Donnelly have shared the screen in four films so far: Friendsgiving, A Week in Paradise, Slayers, and Us or Them. Their first movie together was the 2020 comedy Friendsgiving, in which they played a couple—and even had to film a steamy sex scene. During a 2020 appearance on The Talk, Akerman opened up about filming the “crazy S&M scene.”

“[It was] just like being in our home,” she joked when asked what it was like filming the sex scene. She added that she was glad to have her husband as her costar. “Any chance I get to have him do a scene like that, who better than to do it with than your husband?” she said. “It’s a really, kind of, intimate, crazy scene, and thank God we know each other well enough instead of just meeting somebody on the first day and [doing] this crazy S&M scene. It was lovely to have him there.”

During a November 2026 appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show, Akerman and her The Hunting Wives costar Brittany Snow discussed Snow’s recent engagement to fiancé Hunter Moreno. When Barrymore asked if their significant others got along too, Akerman gushed, “They’re so close!”

“We call them all the Hunting Husbands,” Akerman added, sharing their nickname for all the boyfriends and husbands of the cast.

#6674. The 17 Best Airbnbs in Copenhagen Embrace Hygge

If you’ve spent years saving photos of Copenhagen street style and Danish living rooms, the best way to really experience Scandi fashion and design is to go straight to the source—moodboards can only take you so far. Watch locals pedal past in color-blocked coats and billowy blouses, browse the racks at Hay House, and keep tabs on how many cafés have a Louis Poulsen pendant over their counter. Winter may be cold, but it’s a great time to go and see the city in action. Tivoli Gardens lights up for Christmas and the city settles into the candlelit coziness of hygge season.

A Copenhagen apartment delivers Scandinavian style up close. Think herringbone floors, tall windows, blonde wood, and a kitchen that’s set up to actually cook in. From canal-side flats in Christianshavn to a family house a short bike ride from the center, these are the Copenhagen Airbnbs at the top of our list.

The sunny striped mural in the dining room says it all: This home has personality. This 170-square-meter apartment takes up the first floor of its building and is located in one of the oldest squares in the city, once belonging to a duke. The interiors use warm ochre tones and terrazzo tiles in both bathrooms. French balcony doors open onto a quiet inner courtyard, but for evenings and nights, the square is a cozy place to be, with candlelit restaurant windows (including one right downstairs) just around the corner.

Amenities: Fully equipped kitchen, dressing room, Wi-Fi, TV, free gym access, 24/7 support

Set in an 18th-century house on Amaliegade, a block from Amalienborg Palace, this apartment has high ceilings and old-world details like wood-paneled walls and a large hearth grounding the living room. Step outside and the Marble Church, Designmuseum Danmark, and the noon changing of the guard are just a few minutes’ walk away. If you visit during the holiday season, the Nyhavn Christmas market is just down the street.

Clean lines and a restrained palette rule in this two-bedroom apartment, located right in the middle of most of the city’s big attractions. That’s not to say it doesn’t have its quirks: Look closely, and you’ll notice more than a few duck figurines (as well as a brass pretzel hanging in the kitchen). With a full cooking and dining space, you’ll feel right at home on the nights you want to stay in—and when you don’t, Copenhagen’s best restaurants are right on your doorstep.

Amenities: Washer, TV, sound system, balcony, backyard, outdoor furniture, elevator, EV charger

Though it can technically accommodate up to four with the help of the living room sofa, this spot is ideal for the couple craving solitude. It’s located in Frederiksberg, a more residential city-within-a-city known for its green space, and is itself a charming old wood house. (The fact that its surrounded by a fruit garden only amplifies its oasis-like feel.) Accented by rustic wooden furniture and a cozy fireplace, the whitewashed interiors are anything but stark.

Amenities: Wood-burning fireplace, fire pit, hammock, outdoor dining area, loungers

Somewhere between eclectic treehouse and antique treasure trove, this penthouse apartment definitely makes for a memorable stay—if only for the decor. Between the lacquered paint, bold wallpaper, and personality lighting (the fuchsia fringe lamp in the living room is of particular note), this place will soothe the maximalist traveler uninspired by Scandinavian simplicity. It has a spacious balcony if you’re visiting in the warmer months, and is well-located in the heart of the historic district; City Hall is a quick five-minute walk away.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, TV, balcony, outdoor furniture

Sunny, centrally located, and ideally sized for a couple, this newly renovated apartment is perfect for a first-time stay in Copenhagen. (The space is a five-minute walk from the metro and next to two big supermarkets.) You’ll have access to a shared garden to unwind in the evenings (if your trip is in the summer, the sun doesn’t set until 10 p.m.) and a dining table for nights in when the temperatures dip.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, dryer, TV, dishwasher, shared backyard

Built in 1904, this light-filled apartment is full of historical touches like high ceilings and intricate crown molding. It’s a one-bedroom, but spacious enough so that you can fully stretch out: The living area is divided between a sitting room and an open kitchen-dining room. Fælledparken, the city’s largest park, is conveniently located nearby—be sure to make a pit stop at the famous Juno bakery on your way.

Amenities: TV, washer, dryer, backyard, dishwasher

For a more colorful take on Danish style, stay at this color-blocked three-room in the middle of Nørrebro. Start your day off with a tea on the terrace that’s right off the bedroom before heading out for a day of exploring: You’ll be less than a five minute walk from the lakes, where you’ll find plenty of cafés and shops to peruse.

Amenities: TV, dishwasher, private balcony, shared backyard, paid parking

The tall windows light up a calm, pared-back space with a dining table big enough for group dinners (the space sleeps to 10) and a living room with both a sofa and a daybed for extra guests. The furnishings and fixtures read classic Scandi style. Illum and Hay House are a few minutes’ walk away for shopping, and the holiday market at Højbro Plads is close enough that you can drop your bags at home between rounds of gløgg. Climb the Round Tower’s spiral ramp at dusk for a view of the city.

Amenities: Fully equipped kitchen, dedicated workspace, Wi-Fi, crib and high chair, shared courtyard, small pets allowed

A short 10-minute bike ride out of the center lands you in the Amagerbro district, in the northern (and less touristy) part of the city. With a dining table that can fit six and a large, open-concept kitchen, it's ideal for a group stay.

Amenities: TV, washer, dishwasher, room darkening shades

For a standalone house that's close to the action, opt for this three-bedroom home that’s a five-minute bike ride from Nørrebro. It’s great for longer stays (there’s a desk for remote work, too) and anyone traveling with small children will especially appreciate the backyard. There, you’ll find playhouses, swings, and even a trampoline.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, dryer, TV, crib, pack ’n play, high chair, baby bath, playroom, outdoor playground, fireplace, dishwasher, balcony, private backyard, fire pit, outdoor kitchen, BBQ, bikes, free parking

Nestled amongst wine bars and tiny boutiques, this one-bedroom apartment is in a pretty unbeatable location. A real highlight is the kitchen: those who love to spend hours combing local markets when they travel will find plenty of space to whip up something with fresh ingredients, to be enjoyed either in the dining nook or on the balcony that overlooks the picturesque street.

Amenities: Washer, TV, BBQ, paid parking,

Situated in the old red-light district of Copenhagen—a neighborhood that now functions as a creative hub—this roomy apartment overlooks the main square of Enghave Plads. As such, the balcony provides prime seating for starting and ending each day eavesdropping on the busy streets below; though we can also envision many quieter evenings spend indoors taking advantage of the impressive library.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, TV, outdoor playground, dishwasher, private balcony, backyard, fire pit, BBQ, paid parking

For a weeklong stay, this apartment right near the buzzing street of Jægersborggade (home to around 40 art galleries, vintage shops, and coffee shops) will feel like home. It has a balcony for your very own slice of outdoor living, as well as amenities if you’re traveling with small children.

Amenities: Piano, record player, crib, high chair, outdoor playground, dishwasher, balcony, backyard

Light and airy, this sunny apartment is quintessentially Scandinavian, right down to the wishbone dining chairs and the IKEA storage units. You’ll have access to both a balcony and a backyard during your stay, and homebodies will especially appreciate the cozy touches—from a movie projector for a DIY cinema to a wood-burning stove, this is a vacation rental that’ll feel like your own.

Amenities: Washer, TV, fireplace, dishwasher, balcony, backyard

When you look up the word “hygge” in Pinterest you may as well get a referral to this very image. With low lighting, warm wood furniture, and lots of cushy textiles, this two-floor home is the ultimate cozy stay. During the warmer months, take advantage of the courtyard; it’s a great spot to sit with a glass of wine under the leafy trees.

From the wide-plank floors to the oversized windows to the two (!!) balconies, everything about this bright apartment is charming. Bonus points for the massive green kitchen, where we can imagine kicking off slow mornings with a cup of coffee and maybe a spandauer pastry purchased at one of the many bakeries that line the street below.

Amenities: TV, Dryer in building, dishwasher, shared backyard, outdoor playground, EV charger, paid parking

#6672. A New Azzedine Alaïa Retrospective Goes Beyond the Bandage Dress

The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco examines the great couturier’s legacy

The bandage dress. The zipper dress. The perforated leather. The jersey hoods. The peplummed chemises. Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion. The bandage dress is perhaps the most pervasive bit of his legacy, and it is emblematic of how the late French-Tunisian designer ushered in a new body-conscious silhouette in the ’80s, one made possible by technological innovations in materials that sculpted without any rigid, waist-cinching structure.

Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. She has spent the past four years developing a new exhibition titled “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” the first major U.S. retrospective dedicated to the work of the famed couturier. It opened November 21.

Born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work. In 1956, he decamped to Paris to pursue fashion full-time. After a brief internship at the house of Christian Dior, he worked under Guy Laroche for less than two years before taking on his own private clients, then launching his own atelier in the late ’70s. From there, he built the house we know today. His obsession with construction and material innovation allowed him to both celebrate and liberate the female form. He passed away in late 2017 at the age of 82.

Camerlengo first encountered Alaïa’s work as an assistant on the “Patrick Kelly Runway of Love” exhibition that the Philadelphia Museum of Art organized in 2014. “I was intrigued by how many of the new designers in Paris at this time were being supported by US consumers and retailers,” she says. After ascending to her new position in San Francisco years later, she cold-emailed Olivier Saillard, director of the Azzedine Alaïa Foundation in Paris. He was intrigued, and the two began working together on the exhibition almost immediately.

The exhibition focuses on 80 garments from across Alaïa’s celebrated career, divided over a series of archetypes—the bandage dresses, sculptures and shapes, black and white, silhouettes and suiting, and construction and craftsmanship—to explore how his design aesthetic evolved. Interspersed are designs worn by devotees like Tina Turner, Grace Jones, and Rihanna. One final gallery highlights his personal collections of the work of designers he most admired, like Christian Dior and Charles James.

Ahead, Camerlengo speaks to Bazaar about curating the new exhibition, contextualizing Alaïa’s work in today’s fashion landscape, and his enduring legacy.

The exhibition is not chronological. We look at a series of Alaïa’s archetypes like the bandage dress to explore how his design aesthetic evolved over the course of his career. He often himself said that he didn’t want to conform to seasonal trends; he was more interested in the evolution of his designs. And so the gallery shows a mix of objects dating from the 1980s to his final collection in 2017, and they’re largely grouped by type.

When you come in, you are greeted by Grace Jones, as we say, and the seminal purple hooded bandage dress from the fashion Oscars [a French event held in 1985]. As you move through, you’ll see a selection of the zipper dresses, the chiffon gowns, and other works that tie into some of the other themes. In each space, we mix the time periods. And that was something Alaïa himself often said. [He had a running joke that he didn’t know his own age.] He often said he was “as old as the pharaohs.” Basically, time was a construct for him.

That’s a great word for it. We could think of the popularity of the Japanese fashion designers who obscured women’s bodies with their voluminous styles. We could think of the suiting of the period. The 1970s is this period of workplace equality. Women are wearing suits in the style of masculine dress, but that also means they're obscuring their bodies. And then we can think of pop culture. I always think of Diane Keaton’s Annie Hall in 1977.

Some of the individuals I interviewed for my catalog text who were retailers in San Francisco at the time described Alaïa's designs as being like a whiplash. It was a complete 180 from the styles that they had gotten used to over the past decade, which also includes the rise of T-shirts and jeans for women as a mode of dress.

So here you have these very sexy, very form-fitting clothes. And part of the Alaïa aesthetic, as I see it, is the reclamation of the gaze. Rather than women being passively looked at—usually by men—they are instead commanding their own agency. As you said, it was completely earth-shattering and very shocking at the time.

Azzedine Alaïa was one of the few couturiers who could work completely by the methods of tailoring and by draping, start to finish, from the initial concept to the final product. I did not fully appreciate his tailoring and the suits he constructed beforehand. We have a selection of them in a gallery of the exhibition, and their construction is absolutely incredible. The way they fit the body, the way they uplift and empower women through cloth—again, very antithetical to what we saw in the decades prior in the 1970s. These are very form-fitting, tailored at the waist, but they have soft feminine touches as well that give you this interesting mix of femininity and strength at the same time.

Very important. We talk in the first gallery about how women, speaking generally, were the architects of his life. He learned to sew from his sister, who was working for a seamstress. He was encouraged by a local midwife in Tunisia to go to school at the Institute of Fine Arts. She helped him forge his papers to read 16—he was only 15 at the time. He learned his skills, not in formal training, but from women in Tunisia.

And then his early work was supported by a lot of leading figures of international society, including various Rothschilds, the French performer Arletty, the Swedish American actress Greta Garbo, and that's all before he even started to work formally under his own label in the 1980s. Of course, in the 1980s, he adopts Naomi Campbell, who becomes his protégé. He has close relationships with Grace Jones and Tina Turner. They were hugely important to him. In the exhibition, the clear invisible mounts that we use are actually based on the body of Naomi Campbell.

Probably the Grace Jones bandage dress from the fashion Oscars in 1985. Not only is it the progression of the bandage dress style that he experiments with throughout the course of the 1980s, but it represents a key moment in his career where he receives two very high accolades as part of the fashion Oscars and he’s recognized for his genius.

As far as the designs themselves, I think we would consider the bandage dress, for example, an iconic symbol of late 20th- and 21st-century fashion developed by Azzedine Alaïa, but of course iterated upon extensively. We've seen surges and resurgences in its popularity ever since.

And then as far as the landscape of the broader fashion system, Alaïa was someone who really eschewed seasonal calendars and trends. He was unconcerned with making things for the market. He often wanted to just produce clothes and share them when he felt they were ready. So I think his method of working foreshadows some of the conversations we’re having now about the overproduction of fashion and the overconsumption of fashion, even the detrimental environmental impacts that we see connected to it. He was really a forerunner, in a sense, to question the fashion system.

You can see how he really studied the construction of other garments and then adapted it in his own way in his designs. For example, he admired the work of Charles James, the great American fashion designer who was able to manipulate fabric to achieve weightless volume. And you see in Alaïa's own collections as he continues in his career, he does radial tucks and pleating to also get a certain amount of weightless volume in some of his gowns, very much in the spirit of James.

I hope our visitors appreciate the artistry of his work, first and foremost, and also the importance of handcraftsmanship. We are increasingly in an age of technology, especially with the rise of AI. What he created by his own hand is something that we can really marvel at.

#6671. Your December Horoscope by Zodiac Sign

We’re wrapping up the year with great momentum going into the new year.

December’s astrology helps you wrap the year up with some forward momentum! At the start of the month, the Sun continues its joyful journey through Sagittarius, putting you in a more adventurous mood and encouraging you to expand your horizons and perspective. It's a great time to get in a debate during a holiday dinner and stand up for what you believe in, but to also practice your active listening skills and remain open to the possibility that you could learn something from someone else. You’re zooming out and thinking more about the world around you and eager to soak up life’s experiences by trying new things and meeting new people.

You’re feeling all-or-nothing when it comes to love once Venus moves into Scorpio on December 4. For the next few weeks, Venus is retracing its steps that it took during the retrograde, so you might finally experience relief or turning points regarding some of your key relationships and contracts. This can help you navigate uncomfortable terrain in your close connections with honesty and vulnerability. You’re feeling funnier than normal once Mercury enters Sagittarius on December 6. When our communication planet moves through jokester Sagittarius, your conversations are a bit more playful but words can also sting from time to time. It’s easier to speak what’s on your mind in the moment and regret it later. You might also have a harder time finding a plan or strategy to reach certain goals, but right now you’re not meant to sort through the details. Focus on the big picture and soaking up new information and experiences instead. If you’re traveling, you might also deal with more snafus, so plan accordingly!

A New Moon in Sagittarius on December 8 helps you reconnect with a source of hope or optimism. Conversations feel expansive and information that you learn might inform your worldview in a new way. This energy is also helpful for reframing the way you speak to yourself and releasing limiting beliefs. You might find yourself eager to book some travel or sign up for a workshop to hone a skill or learn something new. You’re not afraid to set firm boundaries when Saturn stations direct in Aries on December 10. This will bring you back to July 26, the day the retrograde began. Similar themes and topics are resurfacing and asking you to be accountable for your own limitations or to set necessary boundaries with courage.

A few days later, on December 12, Neptune stations direct in Aries, helping you to dissolve your ego. This brings you back to July 7, and puts you in touch with certain topics and conversations that were a focus around then. You might feel more tender and sensitive, or feel a burst of creativity. This can help you channel your own creative energy for a higher purpose or ideal to make a positive impact in the collective. On the same day, Jupiter stations retrograde in Leo, bringing a crisis of faith. You could learn news or experience something that rattles your foundation or makes you question your own belief system. This can put you in a philosophical mood, asking you to reflect on whether you’re living in alignment with your beliefs. There might also be developments regarding teachers and mentors in your life, decisions about going back to school, or turning points regarding some of your goals and dreams.

The Sun enters Capricorn on December 21, marking the Winter Solstice in the Northern Hemisphere and the longest night of the year. From now on, the daylight will slowly begin to increase once again. But first, you must move through winter and preserve your precious energy in the process. This is not the time to overdo it or overextend yourself. It’s time to prune people, patterns, and situations from your life that extinguish your drive and essence instead of replenishing them. A Full Moon in Cancer on December 23, highlights your relationship with the past, primary caregivers, and security. There might be significant developments within your chosen family or perhaps you’re making a decision about where you live. People are in a more sentimental mood and the past can stir up major feelings and reflections. Be gentle with yourself and others.

The month wraps up with Mercury entering Capricorn on December 25, lending you a more structured approach to your ideas and communication style. You might find yourself navigating boundaries more or even find yourself speaking with a little more directness. There’s no need to sugarcoat to keep others comfortable, your time is limited and you’ve got things to do! This energy can be productive, help you problem solve, and stick with habits and plans that build toward your longterm success.

Take a deep breath as the mood lightens, the pace picks up, and possibilities begin to look exciting again. Just remember to keep your feet firmly on the ground as you make the most of everything coming your way, because it can be easy to get swept up in all that excitement.

But while Sagittarius season is usually fun for everyone, this year it’ll hit some signs more than others. Below, see if you’re among the luckiest zodiac signs of the season.

Your season is here, and it means increased luck, serendipity, and cosmic blessings. As the sun moves into your sign, you find that classic Sag fire surfacing once again. You’ll feel more motivated and driven, with that go-getter energy making a comeback. Do you care about the spoils of war that had you weeping last season? Not exactly. Your gaze shifts towards those solid relationships and blessings that keep your life moving in all the stable ways. You are no longer waiting for someone else to show you the way ahead. You are back with a bang, and you know exactly where you are headed.

Ideas: check. Finances: check. Self-confidence: check. Aries, you are thriving this Sagittarius season! Life may have thrown you some lemons lately, but you’ve picked up the pieces and turned them into something creative that excites you, mostly because it pushes you to explore life through a fresh lens. You used your season well, Scorpio. You mulled over challenges, ruminated over choices, and tried your best to look at the larger picture. Sagittarius season simply gives wings to all those ideas and shifts you have been plotting silently in your head. You may not be leaping onto the other side just yet, but what you are definitely doing is laying rock-solid foundations for what you are here to build. You’ve set your timelines, fixed your goals, and are now ready to set them into motion.

From conflicting goals to emerging victorious, life has come full circle for you. You stuck to your guns, bit through the challenges, and found your way to the other side. Now that you are here, you feel a renewed sense of energy to build once again, but with greater clarity, sharper vision, and a stronger sense of alignment. Whether it’s in work or relationships, it’s time to play your best hand and give it your all. It’s time to clear the deck and open up to receive. #6664. Who Is Michelle Yeoh’s Husband, Jean Todt?

The motorsports executive has been linked to the Oscar-winning actress since 2004

Michelle Yeoh has spent decades bringing stories to the silver screen—with roles in hit films like Crazy Rich Asians and Wicked to the upcoming Blade Runner 2099—but her love life has a pretty remarkable story of its own.

The Oscar-winning actress married French businessman and former Ferrari CEO Jean Todt in 2023, nearly 19 years after he first proposed. The pair have been together since 2004, supporting each other through career milestones, international travels, and plenty of memorable moments along the way. But who is the man standing by one of Hollywood’s most accomplished actresses?

Ahead, everything you need to know about Yeoh’s husband, Jean Todt, including his career in motorsports, how the couple met, and their long-awaited wedding.

Todt was born on February 25, 1946, in Pierrefort, a commune in France’s South-Central region. He studied at École des Cadres School of Economics and Business in Paris. At 80 years old, he’s 16 years Yeoh’s senior.

Todt is best known for his work in motorsports, but his career actually began behind the wheel—or, more accurately, in the passenger seat. He started as a rally co-driver, a role he held from 1966 to 1981, before moving into the business and management side of racing.

From there, he went on to work with some of the biggest names in the industry. In 1981, he joined Peugeot as its director of racing before founding Peugeot Talbot Sport, where he helped the team secure multiple World Rally Championship titles. In 1993, he moved to Ferrari, eventually becoming the company’s general manager in 2004 and CEO in 2006, a position he held until 2008.

But his career didn’t end with Ferrari. In 2009, Todt was elected president of the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA), the governing body for international motorsports, including Formula One. He held the position for 12 years, until 2021, and has also served as the United Nations secretary general's special envoy for road safety since 2015.

Yeoh and Todt’s love story began in Shanghai, China, in June 2004. Yeoh attended a Ferrari event, where she met Todt, who was then the company’s general manager. According to the couple’s wedding program, they first crossed paths on June 4, 2004, and Todt proposed less than two months later, on July 26. Yeoh said yes, beginning what would become a nearly two-decade engagement.

After nearly 19 years together, Yeoh and Todt finally tied the knot on July 27, 2023, in Geneva, Switzerland, surrounded by family and friends. Brazilian racing driver Felipe Massa first shared the news, posting photos from the celebration on social media. Todt later confirmed the marriage and called Yeoh the love of his life.

The couple’s wedding program included a sweet recap of their relationship, noting that they had met 6,992 days earlier. Yeoh also shared photos from the celebration on Instagram, writing, “19 years and YES!! we are married!!” The actress wore several looks for the occasion, including a champagne-colored gown, and celebrated with loved ones—including her new husband’s colleagues from the world of Formula One.

Todt has one son, Nicolas, from a previous relationship. Born on November 17, 1977, Nicolas has followed in his father’s footsteps, carving out his own career in motorsports. He is a racing manager and talent manager who has worked with some of the sport’s biggest names, including Charles Leclerc and Felipe Massa.

#6662. I Tested Peloton's New, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.)

Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a big, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The new Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex showed up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

In reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

Okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

Treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or big garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.)

This is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.)

None of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

What it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and big at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

On top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the company makes machines for.

The Tread Flex also provides personalized training plans, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

Oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

So, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

How you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's new entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

As a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

Well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

The Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

List price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.
