#6637. Veruschka, the Shape-Shifting Supermodel Who Defined an Era, Has Died at 87

Richard Avedon famously pronounced Veruschka “the most beautiful woman in the world.” But what made the German model so mesmerizing was her seeming disinterest in preserving any one iteration of that beauty. She could be imperious or impish, feral or feline, androgynous or opulently feminine. She could contort her impossibly long limbs into unreal configurations, traversing fashion magazines and the wider public’s consciousness with ease in a way that had never been done before. One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion’s great performance artists.

On November 25 it was confirmed by the German newspaper Bild that the model died at the age of 87, surrounded by friends and family at home.

It was only earlier this month, on the occasion of the release of Ron Howard’s Netflix documentary Avedon, that Vogue revisited an extraordinary 25-page fashion editorial from its March 1, 1967, issue. Across those pages, Veruschka leapt and pirouetted, her hair fashioned into a long, swinging braid by hairstylist Ara Gallant. Avedon had found in Veruschka a woman who could give physical expression to his imagination and whose own imagination was every bit as expansive. Here was a woman whose beauty “demands something, and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever,” said Avedon.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort on May 14, 1939, in Königsberg, East Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia), Veruschka’s early life was marked by the horrors of war. She was five years old when her father, Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, was executed for his involvement in the failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler. The family was imprisoned by the Nazi regime, and the aristocratic world into which she had been born had all but disappeared by the time the war came to an end.

An art student, she was discovered in Florence in 1959. Her early forays into modeling were not immediately fruitful: Standing over six feet tall, she was an unconventional proposition even then. An initial stint in New York proved disappointing, but in Italy she developed a fruitful creative relationship with photographer Johnny Moncada. Some 3,000 images from those formative years, undiscovered for decades, would eventually form the basis of the book From Vera to Veruschka: The Unseen Photographs by Johnny Moncada and an accompanying exhibition at London’s Somerset House in 2014.

Her greatest act of reinvention was, arguably, the creation of Veruschka herself. Adopting the Russian-sounding diminutive of her first name, she cultivated a persona of indeterminate provenance and mystique. Returning to New York in 1964, she found an industry increasingly receptive to her brand of beauty. In Diana Vreeland, then editor in chief of Vogue, she found a kindred spirit.

The 1960s heralded the ascendance of a new breed of model, with the likes of Jean Shrimpton, Twiggy, Donyale Luna, and Penelope Tree becoming cultural figures in their own right. Veruschka, with her high forehead, sculptural cheekbones, and elongated limbs, was one of the decade’s most arresting presences, whatever aesthetic she took on. She appeared on 13 American Vogue covers, working with the likes of Avedon, Irving Penn, Horst P. Horst, and David Bailey, and became one of the highest-paid models of her generation.

Some of her most enduring images were made in collaboration with the Italian photographer Franco Rubartelli, her creative and romantic partner. Among them was the indelible 1968 photograph of Veruschka in Yves Saint Laurent’s lace-up safari jacket for French Vogue, an image that distilled the designer’s new vocabulary of female sensuality and authority.

Veruschka was also an endlessly inventive beauty muse. The Vogue archives are rich with examples of her aesthetic adventurism. She sports fantastical lashes, intricately braided hair, graphic eye makeup, and elaborate headpieces. She was chameleonic, which made her popular with the hair and makeup artists of the era.

And her fame extended well beyond the pages of fashion magazines. In Michelangelo Antonioni’s seminal 1966 film Blow-Up, set in Swinging London, Veruschka played a version of herself in a brief but electrifying scene opposite David Hemmings’s fashion photographer. A year later, she graced the cover of Life magazine. Few models before her had so thoroughly captured the imagination of the wider public, and her legacy lives on in the new generation of celebrity models today.

By the mid-1970s, however, Veruschka had grown disenchanted with the fashion industry. Her artistic ambitions began to take greater precedence over her modeling career. In collaboration with the German artist Holger Trülzsch, she embarked on a captivating body of photographic work in which her painted figure dissolved into architectural surfaces and natural environments, or assumed entirely different identities.

In 1971 Veruschka also appeared in West German magazine Stern with 27 other women under the coverline: “Wir haben abgetrieben!” (“We’ve had abortions!”) to advocate for abortion law reform at a time when it was illegal. It was a significant moment in Germany’s ’70s feminist wave.

Still, fashion never entirely relinquished its fascination with her, nor she with it. There were occasional returns to the runway, including for Chanel in 1994 and, at the age of 71, for Giles Deacon’s spring 2011 show in London. In 2017, Acne Studios enlisted her for its resort 2018 look book. In contemporary photos—with her silver hair slicked back, sporting oversized, louche tailoring—she looks every bit as modern as she had half a century earlier.

Veruschka on the red carpet at the Berlin Film Festival in 2015.

Much has been made of Veruschka’s otherworldliness, but there was something profoundly human in her commitment to metamorphosis. At the height of her fame, she could have made a career out of being the most beautiful woman in the world. How much more interesting, instead, to become a thousand different women.

#6632. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6631. Why Weed Might Actually Be Bad for Your Sleep

Everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a new October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

The study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis users had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis users weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She says more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Deep sleep is one of the most important stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

Not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu says it’s important for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

If you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

#6629. Veruschka: The Late ’60s Supermodel’s Best Beauty Looks of All Time

There are few faces more synonymous with the youthquake of the ’60s than Veruschka, who has sadly passed away at the age of 87.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort in East Prussia, the German countess was discovered at 20 years old while studying art in Florence. Soon after, she decamped to New York City, where she changed her name from Vera to Veruschka and became one of the most—if not the most—in-demand supermodels of the decade, regularly appearing in the pages of Vogue and lensed by greats such as David Bailey, Irving Penn, and Richard Avedon.

Standing six feet tall, she was a bombshell with a chiseled-by-the-gods bone structure, steely blue gaze, plush mouth, and shape-shifting champagne-blonde hair. Her “indomitable career of beauty,” as Susan Sontag once famously deemed it, was characterized by portraits of her sinewy silhouette, immortalized most notoriously in that scene from Michelangelo Antonioni’s cult 1966 film Blow-Up, where she poses for photographer David Hemmings’s camera to amorous effect.

As for her countless evocative close-ups, which showcased her otherworldly hair and makeup looks, nothing was too decorative or directional for Veruschka, and it was this perpetual gameness that made her a favorite of Diana Vreeland during her tenure at Vogue. There were her sculptural, teased-to-the-heavens, and decidedly ’60s hair looks, from a voluminous bouffant with waist-grazing lengths, to an origami-like knot, to the tornado of face-framing braids that she wore in a 1967 editorial shot by her longtime lover and collaborator Franco Rubartelli. And then there were her signature extreme lashes, which ran the gamut from classic, doll-like fringe to cast in Technicolor shades or granddaddy longlegs lengths, and were often punctuated by a sheer wash of pastel pigment on the lids, graphic winged liner, and glossy pink lips.

“The most beautiful woman in the world,” according to Avedon, and a true chameleon in every sense of the word, Veruschka’s metamorphic fluency continues to be a lethal and enduring combination in the fashion world. In fact, in 2017, Acne Studios tapped Veruschka to star in its Resort 2018 look book, where she wore the collection’s cropped jackets and slouchy trousers with a sharp slick back and statuesque swagger. Here, a look at her most striking beauty looks of all time.

#6628. 25 Midwestern Thanksgiving Recipes That Bring The Nostalgia (& The Flavor)

Even nicer than Midwest nice (and that's saying something!).

My holidays were split between regions growing up. We spent Thanksgiving at my dad’s side, and Christmas with my mom’s. With my mom’s Alabama and Texas roots and my dad's Missouri and Kansas roots, that meant that Christmas dinner was a Southern affair and Thanksgiving was a Midwestern feast. Both holiday spreads had a fair amount of overlap of dishes (casseroles galore), but I have to say: A classic Midwest Thanksgiving has a special place in my heart.

What makes a Midwest Thanksgiving, you may ask? All of the classics are present, plus a few surprising favorites that, in my house, no holiday is complete without. We think beyond the turkey, sometimes skip mashed potatoes for a cheesy casserole, and have to be careful not to fill up on all the rolls (butter and honey better be on the table). Ready to celebrate Midwest-style? Here are some recipes that your holiday won’t be complete without:

Made with canned pineapple, pistachio pudding, and Cool Whip, this retro crowd-pleasing dessert “salad” will take you straight back to the ’70s with just one bite. It’s the perfect recipe to throw together if you don’t have a ton of time, but you need to take something to that potluck or family gathering.

Thanksgiving is equally about food and football, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing is a no-brainer. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

It takes less than than 5 minutes to pour some pepper jelly over cream cheese and place some crackers around. These bites are slightly more elevated without many more steps. It’s for those that want to feel like they are putting some effort into their appetizer without it being difficult or time-consuming.

Don't be fooled by the name—the only thing deathly about this casserole is how absolutely delicious it is. This cheesy, creamy casserole is a staple at every holiday in my Kansas home, and Thanksgiving is no exception. Yes, we often have mashed potatoes too.

For this recipe, we ditched canned cream of mushroom soup and went for fresh instead. It's not how my mom makes it, but trust me—by sautéing mushrooms with sliced onion in butter, you're building a base with some serious depth of flavor. Cook the mushrooms enough that they get a little caramelized, and you'll really be good to go.

No matter the holiday, one thing is for sure: Deviled eggs will be making an appearance. Variations are always welcome (looking at you, harissa deviled eggs), but if grandpa is going to have a happy Thanksgiving, then this classic recipe better be present.

Strawberry pretzel tart, AKA strawberry pretzel salad, might sound a little strange, but trust us—it strikes the perfect balance of whimsical and classic, sweet and salty. The pretzel crust proves to be an ideal complement to the rich cream cheese layer and the sweet strawberries with their Jell-O glaze.

Turkey usually rules the roost at Thanksgiving, but it's not the only centerpiece present at many Midwestern holiday tables. Depending on how many family members are coming, my family has been known to prepare a turkey and a ham—it's the best of both worlds!

We’re certainly not opposed to roasted Brussels sprouts, but we also love giving them the traditional Thanksgiving treatment—plenty of butter, cream, and cheese. This method upgrades even the most humble vegetables while still allowing them to be the star of the show.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for. Plus, you can easily make it ahead and travel with it, making it an ideal potluck recipe.

Essentially, this is chicken Alfredo, but with a few extra decadent add-ins, like cream cheese, garlic, and punchy spices like nutmeg and black pepper. When you’re craving the classic but have to serve a crowd, this is the recipe you should make.

A cheese ball is peak party appetizer nostalgia, and these cheese ball bites are here to put a new, shareable twist on the classic. They’re so simple to make, only require a handful of ingredients, and are super versatile based on what you have on hand.

Traditional stuffing should be stuffed inside the turkey and cooked in there, but in my family, we've always called it stuffing. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath.

What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato, of course. With this in mind, we combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for.

#6626. Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a new bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” says Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” says Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any new or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” says Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

“This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

When hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” says Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”

Blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

This condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

If you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any new, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” says Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”

#6625. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6622. Popeyes Beat KFC In My Chicken Sandwich Showdown—But Can It Take Down Chick-fil-A?

The chicken sandwich wars are far from over.

Few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich. And while plenty of chains have introduced their own versions over the years, Chick-fil-A and Popeyes remain two of the biggest names in the conversation.

In my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich. Popeyes ultimately came out on top, thanks to its bold seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings. This time, I’m putting Popeyes up against one of its biggest competitors: Chick-fil-A.

Chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

Chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. The pickles also do their job, adding just enough acidity and crunch to balance out the richness.

My biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be said for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

Popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it launched in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

The mayo was another important part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

While Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

Chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

Chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.

#6621. How Did This 14-Year-Old Get Sam Bankman-Fried on the Phone?

Journalists who’ve been anxious about losing their jobs to artificial intelligence would be wise to focus on a different, altogether less menacing but equally impressive threat: 14-year-old Eli Goldfine, the shoestring podcaster from Westchester County who last week conducted a 90-minute interview with Sam Bankman-Fried, who’s currently serving a 25-year sentence in federal prison for orchestrating a multi-billion-dollar cryptocurrency grift.

So how, exactly, does this precocious ninth grader with braces—and not a reporter from one of the scores of legacy publications who’d surely be gunning for access to the disgraced cryptocurrency king—score an interview so coveted? “I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam’s account,” Goldfine, who hosts a podcast about prediction markets called The Supercycle, told me earlier this week. “I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case.”

Goldfine’s classmates are impressed, too, even though he’s been on the receiving end of some gentle ribbing about his on-air ad reads. But can any of them say they got Bankman-Fried to speculate on the likelihood that AI will bring about the extinction of the human race? ("Less than 50%, more than 10%," by the way). Before school’s out for Thanksgiving break, Goldfine joined GQ to talk about his media diet, dream interview subject, and the mechanics of interviewing a man behind bars.

So I learned more about it and I started trading on a fake-money version of Polymarket.

I mean, probably not. I don't have anything against it per se, because people spend money for entertainment on other things. I mean, this is another way to spend your money. But it's not as valuable as prediction markets in some other categories. Right?

I mean, I think I've just always had a motivation to learn more about what I'm interested in. So for news, mostly Bloomberg. For social media, mostly Twitter. And then I also read articles on Substack.

#6620. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6617. Can Your Home Boost Your Endorphins? 7 Simple Tips for a Healthier, Happier Living Space

On a recent cold Sunday morning, I had no interest in doing anything except hiding from the world. Then I did a few small tasks that completely shifted my mood. First, I spritzed a home fragrance with notes of orange and cinnamon around my apartment; next, I raised the blinds to let in some sunlight and tidied up the living room—clearing away clutter, folding blankets, and fluffing the pillows on the couch. As I did, I recalled the words of Loewe’s perfumer, Nuria Cruelles, about one of her candles: “It has the power to transform your house into a home.” That’s exactly what I was doing, simply by adding a bit of scent and straightening up. Another expert, Dr. Rodrigo Arteaga, explains that anyone can turn their home into a “place that improves their health” by following a few simple habits.

There are indeed many small routines we can adopt to turn our home—the place where we relax and let our guard down—into an environment that fosters well-being. Psychologist María Martínez echoes this, encouraging people to practice the Japanese philosophy of kaizen, which emphasizes the transformative power of making gradual, continuous improvements to our lives. “It’s important to create an environment where you look around and like what you see,” she says. “This releases endorphins and makes you feel good. If instead, everywhere you look, there’s a reminder of a task you need to do, something unattractive, or clutter that causes stress, you’ll end up feeling worse. If it gets bad enough, you’ll soon stop wanting to be in your own home. You’ll find reasons to leave or stay late at the office, coming home only to sleep. These are all signs that you need to make changes—not just in your life, but in your home, which should serve as a sanctuary where you can recharge.”

Here are seven practical tips to help create a home environment that helps boost your mental and physical health.

When Florence Pugh was asked in a recent Vogue interview what a perfect day off looks like for her, one of the first things she mentioned was buying flowers. “I love going to my florist and putting together a beautiful bouquet; it makes me so happy,” she said. She’s not alone. According to a study by Dr. Nancy Etcoff of Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, flowers ward off worry, anxiety, and sadness. Study participants felt noticeably better after having flowers in their homes for just a few days—and tended to place them in the kitchen, dining room, and living room, the spaces where they spent most of their time.

Whenever possible, open your curtains and blinds in the morning. As Dr. Arteaga points out, “This gives your brain a powerful signal to synchronize its biological clock. Natural light helps your body recognize when it’s day and when it’s night, giving you more energy during the daytime and helping you rest better at night.” After dusk, create “light islands” inspired by the Danish philosophy of hygge, which offers plenty of ideas for designing a wellness-focused home. As Meik Wiking explains in his book My Hygge Home, you can bring warmth to dark corners of a living room using lamps that cast light downward and bulbs that emit a soft, warm glow. Floor or table lamps placed near a sofa or reading chair work especially well. For more general lighting in spaces meant for relaxation, hygge experts recommend ceiling or wall fixtures with glass or fabric shades that diffuse light gently, rather than harsh overhead chandeliers or pendants.

Studies show that listening to music you love provides an immediate boost to your well-being. “Music has an instant, almost magical effect on us,” explains psychologist Marta Calderero. “Within just a few seconds of hearing a favorite song, your brain is flooded with endorphins and oxytocin. That’s why you suddenly feel that rush of euphoria and such an intimate connection to a track. And it doesn’t stop there—after a couple of minutes, the brain begins releasing dopamine, making us enjoy each second a little more than the last. It’s the most beautiful way I know to regulate emotions and reconnect with the present moment.”

Hygge inspired another recommendation on our list. As Wiking explains, styling a small corner of your home with cozy lighting, blankets (a hygge staple), pillows, a plush rug, and a few favorite objects creates a dedicated spot to unplug from the world. It’s a simple way to build an inviting nook that signals to your brain that you’re in a safe space where it’s okay to relax and unwind.

Going barefoot indoors is another of Dr. Arteaga’s recommendations, and Beatriz Crespo, an expert in healthy micro-habits, seconds the idea. Beyond its physical perks—like improved circulation and balance—walking barefoot reduces stress and encourages relaxation through direct contact between the ground and the nerve-rich soles of your feet.

Proper ventilation offers clear microbiological benefits, as biologist María Dolores Cima Cabal explains: “It helps reduce the density of microorganisms that accumulate inside the home.” At the same time, it delivers real psychological perks, since breathing fresh air reenergizes the body and supplies oxygen to the brain. A Harvard University study confirms that cognitive function can suffer—and reaction times slow down—in stuffy environments.

Returning to that chilly Sunday morning at the start of this piece, candles have a unique ability to turn a house into a home through the evocative power of scent. When you choose an appealing fragrance—whether as a room spray or a candle—your brain registers it as a cue that you’re somewhere you can let your guard down. “Smell is the sense that most powerfully triggers memories, and the one our brain responds to with the greatest intensity,” concludes Calderero. “It forms a direct link between a scent and an emotion. If you keep a signature scent at home, that olfactory connection becomes so strong that the moment you smell it, your brain associates it with rest, comfort, and warmth. Choosing a specific fragrance helps your brain recognize that it’s in a space where it doesn’t need to stay on high alert—and your nervous system naturally slows down.”

#6615. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6612. Still, No One Does Thanksgiving Style Quite Like 'Gossip Girl’s' Blair Waldorf

With my sincerest apologies to Vogue staffers’ favorite pairs of eating pants, when it comes to Thanksgiving fashion, nothing beats the fresh-off-the-runway and fabulous pieces found in Gossip Girl’s now-legendary Thanksgiving episodes. When there’s a svelte Fendi suit or a tapestry McQueen dress on hand, who needs a forgiving drawstring waistband?

Nearly twenty years after the show’s debut, the finer details of those episodes’ familial dramas may be a little murky in memory, but nothing remains as crystal clear as Blair Waldorf’s sharply-defined, uptown girl style. See, for example, the sparkly fall 2007 Marc by Marc Jacobs babydoll dress she dons in season one (episode nine, “Blair Waldorf Must Pie!”). “It’s a defining look for both the character and the show, and I have spent the better part of two decades trying to duplicate it,” says People Like You author and Gossip Girl fashion expert Tyler McCall. “And if you don’t believe that it’s iconic, try and find that dress on the secondhand market for anything close to a reasonable price.”

Blair Waldorf-approved Marc by Marc Jacobs dresses may not have quite reached the CBK-Calvin Klein craze, but do a cursory search, and that particular babydoll dress is still incredibly difficult to procure. But when paired with a knit capelet, bow-printed tights, and a dainty pair of pumps—as it was in the episode—Miss Waldorf’s holiday style could be easily mistaken for the secondhand wishlist of many fashion girls today.

Season 6: Fendi suit, Gucci blouse, Chloé overcoat.

Another treasured Thanksgiving look of Blair’s includes season two’s backless green dress from the now-shuttered label Alexandra Vidal, topped off by a blue Sretsis dress (worn as a coat!) and some seriously autumnal Jimmy Choo boots. However, when it comes to rivaling the babydoll dress, it’s season three’s Nanette Lepore belted tweed coat, worn over a brown printed Sariah dress, and—once again—statement tights that handily take second place. Today, thanks to Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel, not-your-mother’s tweed is all the rage.

While vintage fashion has had us all in a chokehold for quite some time now, and the runways today resemble twenty years ago more than they did ten, McCall also points out how these looks are in lind with certain trends today, including statement tights ,which have re-entered the fashion conversation. (See from the spring 2027 collections: Jil Sander, Marc Jacobs, Lii, and more.) “Festive tights were a Gossip Girl signature, and that’s a trend that’s stuck around for a few winters now, whether it’s a patterned style or a monochromatic moment,” she says. But still, if you’re looking for something a little less uptown, she recommends channeling one of Serena van der Woodsen’s many silky jewel-toned frocks and tapping into the “lingerie-as-daywear” redux. Somehow, Gossip Girl’s Thanksgiving episodes are a time capsule that captures how all great fashion eventually comes back around.

#6610. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6608. We Tried 6 Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies—These Are The Only 2 Worth Serving At Thanksgiving

A handful of things are non-negotiable at Thanksgiving. You need turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and, of course, a slice of pie to round out your meal. And pumpkin pie is the undeniable star of the dessert table.

But sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

It primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That said, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

The pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

Once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez said, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”

Costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she said.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.

And while the sight of one of the original ’90s glamazons in plaid shirts and cowboy boots might once have seemed incongruous, Liz Hurley seems to have taken naturally to life on the country singer’s Tennessee ranch. These days, she looks every bit as at home in a pair of 501s as she does in a cut-out bodycon gown—whether or not the occasion calls for one.

#6605. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6599. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6595. The Luxury Business of Las Vegas F1 Is Booming

If Formula 1 circuits were Mario Kart race tracks, the Las Vegas Grand Prix is as spiritually close to Rainbow Road as it gets.

This year, newly hybrid-engined F1 cars zoomed along an LED-lit Vegas Strip that had been closed off to civilian traffic each night of the event, much to the chagrin of every ride-share driver and/or tourist trying to cross Las Vegas Boulevard. They whipped past the Paris hotel casino’s glittering facsimile of the Eiffel Tower and the cartoonishly massive Sphere. They skirted under banners advertising Louis Vuitton and Qatar Airways. At the end, winner Max Verstappen was driven in a racing-striped stretch limousine, operated by a dashingly bedraggled Keanu Reeves, to the Fountains of Bellagio—inspired, like so many Vegas landmarks, by the architectural grandeur of Europe.

Max Verstappen, shortly after his win on Saturday night.

Motorsports enthusiast Keanu Reeves, center, drove the winners in a limo.

Since the Vegas GP was first revived in 2023, it has been a polarizing stop on the globe-trotting F1 calendar. (Back then, Verstappen called it “99 percent show and 1 percent sporting event.”) Even for a multibillion-dollar sport, was this too much glitz? Surrounded by sandy desert and snow-capped mountains, the gaudiest track in Formula 1 is nevertheless a sight to behold—and this year, it produced one of the most thrilling races in recent memory. Plus, as far as metropolises go, there are certainly more boring places to spend a few days than Sin City.

The winners’ podium: Red Bull’s Verstappen in first, followed by McLaren pair Lando Norris, left, and Oscar Piastri.

Well, unless you’re Kimi Antonelli, F1’s baby-faced world champ.

“The thing I like the most here is the track, because I’m not allowed to do anything else other than drive around,” Antonelli told me, with a smirk, ahead of the race last week. “Because I’m not 21.”

(The Italian, who turned 20 in August, became Formula 1’s youngest-ever world champion at the Mexico Grand Prix earlier this month. In Vegas, he and his Mercedes teammate George Russell just missed the podium, finishing fourth and ninth respectively after more than a few late-race heartbreaks.)

Mercedes drivers Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

But if you’re too old to wait in the line outside Marquee, there were plenty of other desirable libations afoot. Vegas has always been a place where fine cuisine (or at least, high-roller cuisine) means bumping up prices by dumping truffles and caviar on everything. The OG greats of modern dining—the Jean-Georges Vongerichtens and Wolfgang Pucks—have been here since the ’90s. But since COVID, a new generation of big-brass restaurateurs have set up shop on the Strip: Carbone Riviera and the Corner Store at the Bellagio’s properties; Sartiano’s and Delilah at the Wynn; Mother Wolf and Contramar at the Fontainebleau. (There are elite members’ clubs, too: Zero Bond opened at the Wynn in March.)

Brunch at Sadelle's, a popular Major Food Group spot, inside the Bellagio.

During Friday’s qualifying run, former F1 star Daniel Ricciardo stopped by the Corner Store at the Cosmopolitan, a wood-paneled outpost of the New York hotspot that opened a few weeks earlier. In the moody, multi-room space, the kitchen sends out platters of dry-aged wagyu and pepperoni pizza rolls while bartenders shake up sour-cream-and-onion martinis served with potato-chip sidecars. (The cocktail is purportedly Taylor Swift’s favorite, though executive chef Michael Vignola will neither confirm nor deny this: “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” said Vignola, grinning. “You can also ask Travis.”)

A day earlier, Ricciardo—who retired from F1 last year but came to town for a self-branded clothing pop-up and bar at the Bellagio—reflected on his own experience at the first-reprised Vegas GP in 2023. “It feels like a video game,” he said. “Whether the track is your favorite or not your favorite in terms of the actual layout, it’s still pretty surreal to be here and be the main event in a city that revolves around entertainment.”

According to Vignola, Ricciardo is a big fan of the Corner Store’s steak program as well as the chicken paillard, “a sleeper on the menu and a great mid-course this year.” Manning the kitchen at the Corner Store in Vegas, which has 100 more seats than the original NYC location, the chef said they’re selling about as much caviar here as they do in Manhattan.

“Because of the volume here, we are slightly selling a little bit more caviar, slightly, you know, maybe 2 to 1,” Vignola said with a laugh. Lately, they’ve started R&D’ing some Norwegian king crab legs, including a prototype for a “crab appletini.” They’re leaning into menu items that the New York-born chef described as “a little bit more Vegas, flashy kind of bespoke things. There are some high-roller dishes that pop off.”

An Elvis impersonator at F1's Paddock Club.

The likes of Vignola and Mario Carbone, as well as the actual Wolfgang Puck and Jean-Georges, hosted caviar-filled pop-up stands at the Bellagio Fountain Club suites during the F1 festivities. The starriest celebrities, including Reeves and Kim Kardashian, who’s dating driver Lewis Hamilton, watched the big race from the paddock, with a good view of the Elvis impersonator and humanoid robots who roamed the asphalt.

Over my few days in Vegas, multiple locals—including chefs, service and casino employees, and Uber and Lyft drivers—described how the city’s changed over the last 15 years. On the ride from the airport, my driver pointed to a new landmark on the horizon: a massive mirrored edifice shaped like the body of a guitar (the new Hard Rock Las Vegas hotel) that’s in the midst of being erected from the sand.

“I think Vegas and Formula 1, they were meant for each other,” said José Andrés, the Spanish-born chef who opened his first Las Vegas restaurants inside the then-freshly built Cosmopolitan in 2010. “I came here three weeks before the casino opened. And just to watch a casino open is the closest thing to watching a little egg hatch, or my daughter [being] born. For me to watch an entire casino from nothing to becoming a tower, it brings good memories.”

One can only imagine how we’ll look back on the Las Vegas Grand Prix—only in its fourth year—a decade or two from now, when all the cars are self-driving and the Strip has been converted into an actual rainbow speedway floating in deep space. Will there still be Champagne?

#6593. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6592. 11 Best Lab-Grown Diamonds 2026: Fine Jewelry to Engagement Rings

“Lab-grown diamonds are the great equalizer,” says Jean Dousset, the great-grandson of Louis Cartier who pivoted his namesake label to exclusively lab-grown stones in 2023. “People don’t have to compromise anymore to own something exceptional.” Once considered the understudy to mined diamonds, these stones (and therefor, the best ​lab-grown diamond brands), have officially taken center stage—and they’re not just performing, they’re dazzling. Lab-grown diamonds are real diamonds. Not simulants, not stand-ins. We’re talking pure carbon, identical in chemical, physical, and optical makeup to what’s been pulled from the earth for centuries—just made in a lab, not dug up from a mine.

So why the lingering hesitation? Stigma, mostly. The kind passed down like an heirloom from an era when “real” luxury was defined by scarcity and secrecy. But times—and tastes—have changed. “I started working with lab-grown diamonds because it was a smarter, more conscious choice,” says Jennifer Fisher, who now incorporates them across her fine jewelry designs. “They offer the same brilliance and clarity—but they align with how I want to shop and design today.” In an article that ran earlier this year, Jessica Sailer, former Vogue editor and founder of the new lab-grown line Pietro offered this: “Imagine if Hermès introduced an AI technology that could produce a perfect Birkin bag using the same materials in the same atelier, but in a fraction of the time. The craftsmanship would be identical. Would you want one?” Why, yes; yes, of course!

That sentiment is echoed by a growing number of designers (and their clients) who love that you can go bigger, bolder, and cleaner—ethically and aesthetically—without inflating the price tag.

Of course, the Four Cs still matter—color, cut, clarity, and carat—but so do the other Cs: conscience, customization, and carbon footprint. Whether you're buying a diamond ring for a fiancée, a friend, or yourself (because yes, self-gifting is a love language), lab-grown diamonds offer a compelling—and undeniably glamorous—case for the future of fine jewelry. Ahead, discover the 11 best places to shop for lab-grown diamond jewelry, from dainty necklaces to diamond earrings to show-stopping statement pieces.

In the realm of fine jewelry, Kinn stands out as a purveyor of modern heirlooms designed to transcend fleeting trends. Founded in 2017 by Jennie Yoon, Kinn was born from a deeply personal mission: to recreate and reimagine her family’s stolen antique jewelry. This intimate origin story infuses each piece with a sense of continuity and timelessness, aiming to be cherished across generations.

Kinn’s collection seamlessly blends classic elegance with contemporary minimalism. From meticulously crafted engagement rings and wedding bands to everyday essentials like the Solis ring—a bestseller featuring an elegant ribbed design inspired by Yoon's mother’s vintage pleated ring—each piece embodies a narrative of heritage and modernity. Crafted in Los Angeles, the brand works with recycled gold and offers both lab-grown and natural diamonds.

Nearly a decade after launching the business, Yoon continues to build on the idea that a family heirloom needn't be inherited to have sentimental value. The result is jewelry that feels as though it might have belonged to your grandmother, while looking entirely at home in your own jewelry box.

At Vogue World: Milano, Anok Yai even took to the runway in a bespoke Pandora necklace and earrings featuring a lab-grown diamond Mystic Eye charm. Quite the evolution from the charm bracelets of yesteryear.

The brand’s lab-grown diamond offerings, introduced in 2022, are similarly geared toward a new generation of jewelry lovers, with tennis bracelets, delicate studs, and rings that make diamonds feel less like a once-in-a-lifetime purchase and more like an everyday indulgence.

Taylor Swift famously wore Dorsey earrings during her All Too Well short film, giving the brand a front-row seat to pop culture history. Hailey Bieber, Bella Hadid, and Emily Ratajkowski are also admirers, layering Dorsey's white sapphires and lab-grown diamonds with enviable ease.

Jean Dousset may be the great-grandson of Louis Cartier, but his career has never been about resting on pedigree. To help guide your shopping journey, we tapped four jewelry experts to answer the most frequently asked questions about lab-grown diamonds. From the science behind the sparkle to their ethical implications, consider this your lab-grown cheat sheet.

Lab-grown diamonds aren’t new, per se. The technology has been around for decades – General Electric produced the first batch in 1954 – but early versions were largely industrial-grade, used for cutting tools, not rings. Only in the last decade has quality and accessibility caught up with demand. “The technology around lab-grown diamonds had been going on for a long time,” says Jean Dousset, “but had not reached the quality that it did a few years back.”

By the time the Gemological Institute of America (GIA) began grading lab-grown diamonds using the same scale as natural diamonds, Dousset knew the tide was turning: “That was a big breakthrough. The foremost authority in diamond grading acknowledging that these are two diamonds that are the same – with a different origin – meant the product was viable.”

What is a lab-grown diamond? Are lab-grown diamonds real diamonds?

“Lab-grown diamonds are molecularly exactly the same as mined diamonds. In 2018, the FTC updated their definition of what a diamond is, reflecting that lab-grown diamonds are indeed ‘real’ diamonds,” says Strachan. “The only difference between a lab-grown diamond and a mined diamond is the setting in which it’s created – under heat and pressure in a controlled lab setting versus under heat and pressure in the earth.”

Lab-grown diamonds undergo the same formation process, just at warp speed in a lab. There are two primary methods to forming lab-created diamonds:

High Pressure High Temperature (HPHT): Mimics Earth’s natural diamond formation process using a small diamond seed, subjected to over 1.5 million pounds per square inch of pressure and temperatures above 2,000°F.

Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD): Places a diamond seed into a vacuum chamber filled with carbon-rich gas. The gas is heated until the carbon atoms crystallize on the seed, layer by layer.

"The ability to create diamonds in the lab means growers can control for the desired color, cut, clarity, and size,” says Strachan.

However, it’s worth noting that the process requires significant energy input. According to the Natural Diamond Council, CVD methods can consume 250-750 kWh of electricity per carat – comparable to running an average U.S. household for a month. The energy footprint varies widely depending on the lab’s source (renewable vs. fossil fuel).

How can you tell the difference between the best lab-grown diamonds and natural diamonds?

With the naked eye, “it’s nearly impossible to tell the difference between mined and lab-grown diamonds,” says Strachan. “Only a gemologist with the most trained eye is able to tell the difference, and even this is currently under scrutiny,” she adds. “I hear from many Dorsey customers that they layer a Dorsey lab-grown necklace next to a mined diamond necklace, and no one can tell the difference.”

What is the highest grade of lab-grown diamonds?

Lab-grown diamonds can reach the highest grades of Flawless (FL) or Internally Flawless (IF) clarity, D color, and Super Ideal Cut. However, achieving these top grades remains rare.

“Although lab diamond technology has advanced tremendously, the highest color and clarity grades, such as D/FL and D/IF, are still difficult to achieve,” says Annie Chen, Brilliant Earth’s senior vice president of merchandising.

Absolutely. Cut, color, clarity, and carat weight remain essential considerations when buying a lab-grown diamond, just as they are for a mined stone. What has changed is how certain laboratories communicate those qualities. In October 2025, the Gemological Institute of America introduced a new assessment system for eligible lab-grown diamonds, classifying them as either Premium or Standard rather than using its traditional natural-diamond grading nomenclature. Other laboratories, including IGI, continue to provide detailed grading reports using the familiar 4 Cs. In either case, it's worth looking beyond carat weight alone: a beautifully cut diamond can be far more captivating than a larger stone with less sparkle.

There’s no simple answer here. “Value,” as Fisher puts it, “isn’t always about resale.” The jewelry market still treats mined diamonds as rarer, and thus more valuable, but as Dousset points out, “Just because something costs less doesn’t mean it’s cheap. It’s about access – being able to buy the ring you actually want.”

“Symbolically, the fact that we’re not digging into the ground to unearth diamonds resonates,” says Dousset. While lab diamonds still require significant energy, some labs operate entirely on renewable power and produce zero emissions.

The better question may be: what’s the overall impact of a company’s operations? “It comes down to traceability,” says Chen. “That’s where the ethics lie.”
